title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS), also known as central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis, is a rare, inflammatory disorder affecting the blood vessels of the brain and spinal cord, without systemic involvement or underlying connective tissue disease. This course reviews the clinical manifestations of PACNS and potential etiologies. PACNS presents with a wide range of nonspecific symptoms, most commonly focal neurologic deficits, severe persistent headaches, and cognitive impairment. Additional manifestations can include ataxia, seizures, psychiatric or amnestic disorders, visual changes, and, rarely, spinal cord involvement. The etiology remains unclear, though infectious triggers such as Varicella zoster and amyloid deposition have been implicated in subsets of patients. Diagnostic studies that rely on a combination of cerebrospinal fluid analysis, imaging, and, sometimes, brain biopsy are also discussed, as early recognition is critical for the timely initiation of immunosuppressive therapy. Furthermore, maintenance therapy with azathioprine or mycophenolate and vigilant monitoring are recommended to manage disease progression and reduce relapse.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity explores the recognition, diagnosis, and management of PACNS. Participants will gain an understanding of the differentiation of PACNS from secondary CNS vasculitis and other mimicking conditions, the interpretation of cerebrospinal fluid and advanced imaging findings, and the development of individualized treatment plans using induction and maintenance immunosuppressive therapies. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying PACNS, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this rare and complex neurologic disorder to optimize patient outcomes.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the most common presentations of primary angiitis of the central nervous system. Determine the challenges inherent in diagnosing primary angiitis of the central nervous system. Develop up-to-date strategies for the management of primary angiitis of the central nervous system. Collaborate with members of the interprofessional team to achieve earlier diagnosis of primary angiitis of the central nervous system, enabling timely treatment and improved patient outcomes. title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Introduction
content: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS), also known as central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis, is a rare inflammatory disorder of the blood vessels of the brain and spinal cord, without any evidence of systemic vasculitis or an inflammatory or connective tissue disease. PACNS was first described as a distinct clinical entity in 1959, and since then, multiple different clinical presentations have been reported. Manifestations of PACNS at the time of diagnosis are nonspecific, with a wide range of presenting symptoms. The most common presenting manifestations are focal neurologic complaints. These may include weakness, aphasia, and visual field defects. Severe, persistent headaches are also common, as are cognitive decline and encephalopathy. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Etiology
content: The etiology and pathogenesis of PACNS remain unknown, although infectious agents, eg, Varicella zoster , have been proposed as potential triggers. This hypothesis stems from the observation of granulomas in some biopsy specimens of patients diagnosed with the disease. The rarity of PACNS limits opportunities for extensive investigation in this area. [9]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Etiology
content: PACNS also shows a notable association with cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), despite representing a distinct disease process. Amyloid deposition has been identified as a possible trigger for PACNS in animal models. A specific subset of PACNS associated with CAA, termed amyloid-β-related angiitis, appears to involve β-amyloid deposits that provoke an inflammatory response, suggesting a mechanistic link between amyloid pathology and vascular inflammation in these patients. [10] [11] [12] [13] [9]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Epidemiology
content: Studies describing the epidemiology of PACNS, a rare disorder, have not been conducted, and the only available data indicate an annual incidence rate of 2.4 cases per 1 million person-years. [1] The disorder appears to be equally distributed between males and females, with a median age of diagnosis of approximately 50 years. [14]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Pathophysiology
content: The etiology of PACNS remains unknown and is considered a noninfectious process. Inflammation of the central nervous system blood vessels appears to result from immune system activation, with T cells playing a central role in response to various triggers. Immunohistochemical analysis of biopsy samples demonstrates extensive infiltration of CD45R0 + T cells around small cerebral arteries. Matrix metalloproteinases, particularly MMP-9, have been identified as key effector molecules in animal models of PACNS. Additional evidence indicates a dysregulated alternative pathway of complement activation in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from biopsy-confirmed cases, suggesting multiple mechanisms contribute to vascular inflammation.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Pathophysiology
content: Amyloid-β-related angiitis represents a spontaneous PACNS subtype directed against the amyloid-β peptide. This form induces leptomeningeal and parenchymal inflammation, disrupts amyloid-β clearance, and leads to excessive deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels. [15] These processes result in vascular wall inflammation, obstruction of cerebral blood flow, ischemia, and tissue infarction, with occasional hemorrhage. Endothelial dysfunction further accelerates vascular occlusion, while changes in vessel tone exacerbate ischemic injury. [9]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Histopathology
content: Histopathology in PACNS shows small- and medium-vessel vasculitis affecting parenchymal and leptomeningeal arteries. Three different types of vasculitic patterns have been described in PACNS. These include granulomatous, necrotizing, and lymphocytic subtypes. The most common type, granulomatous, shows mononuclear inflammation, granulomas, and multinucleated cells within blood vessel walls. The second most common subtype is lymphocytic, characterized by predominantly lymphocytic infiltration without granulomas. The least common subtype is necrotizing. Vessel wall inflammation is transmural and characterized by fibrinoid necrosis. [9]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features
content: PACNS should be suspected in several clinical scenarios, including patients presenting with multifocal infarctions across different vascular territories without traditional stroke risk factors, patients with chronic aseptic meningitis, or patients exhibiting focal neurologic deficits or diffuse neurologic dysfunction accompanied by brain imaging suggestive of vascular inflammation. [16]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features
content: The onset of PACNS typically occurs insidiously, with a slowly progressive course, although acute presentations have been reported less frequently. Multiple symptoms often appear at initial presentation. Systematic reviews identify focal neurologic signs as the most common presenting feature, followed by headache and cognitive impairment, while other studies highlight headache, altered cognition, and focal weakness as predominant. [7] [17] Additional manifestations can include ataxia, seizures, vertigo, fever, intracranial hemorrhage, psychiatric or amnestic disorders, and visual disturbances, eg, visual field defects, blurred vision, or decreased visual acuity. [18] Spinal cord involvement may present as myelopathy, and rare presentations can mimic brain tumors. A combination of symptoms typically occurs, and PACNS should always be considered in cases of rapidly progressive cognitive decline or unexplained personality changes.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features
content: A comprehensive review of systems and detailed history should assess for systemic conditions associated with secondary CNS vasculitis, including infectious or autoimmune disorders. Supportive findings may include fevers, sinopulmonary disease, cough, joint pain or swelling, rash, hematuria, or proteinuria. History of exposure to infectious agents or toxic substances, as well as recent travel, should also be obtained. Physical examination should align with neurologic complaints and correlate with radiologic findings to guide diagnosis.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation
content: Diagnosis of PACNS is difficult due to the absence of a specific biomarker and the nonspecific nature of the presenting symptoms.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Evaluation
content: The only useful laboratory investigation is CSF examination, which shows an abnormality in more than 90% of cases. A mild increase in leukocyte count (>5 cells/mL), total protein (>45 mg/dL), or both is observed in the majority of cases with normal glucose. However, the usefulness of the CSF is in evaluating for mimickers of CNS vasculitis, including infections and malignancies. [16] CSF studies, including culture and viral PCR, are critical for evaluating an occult infection. More recently, metagenomic next-generation sequencing has emerged as a sensitive technique for infectious workup. A study of nosocomial CSF infections found that 69% of samples were abnormal by metagenomic next-generation sequencing compared with 7.7% that were abnormal by conventional CSF culture. [19] Studies to evaluate for malignancy may include cytology, flow cytometry, or PCR for clonal disorders.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Radiographic evaluation plays a critical role in the diagnosis of PACNS. Abnormal MRI findings, particularly ischemic changes, appear in over 90% of cases, while hemorrhages occur less frequently. [20] [21] [22] [23] [9] Computed tomography angiography (CTA) and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) often serve as first-line imaging studies, but cerebral angiography remains the gold standard. European Stroke Organization guidelines recommend digital subtraction angiography (DSA) over MRA or CTA when clinical suspicion for PACNS is high. [24] DSA demonstrates greater sensitivity for detecting vasculitis in medium-sized vessels, and if MRA or CTA results appear normal, proceeding to DSA is advised. [7] Angiographic abnormalities commonly include alternating segments of stenosis and normal or dilated vessels, as well as arterial occlusions in medium and large vessels.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: High-resolution vessel wall imaging (HRV-MRI) has emerged as a supplementary diagnostic tool, capable of identifying vessel wall pathology beyond luminal changes. Concentric enhancement of the vessel wall represents the most frequently observed feature supporting a PACNS diagnosis using this modality. [25] [26] Despite its potential, HRV-MRI has not yet been adopted as a standard-of-care diagnostic procedure.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation -- Role of brain biopsy
content: Imaging cannot detect small-vessel vasculitis, and if the suspicion for vasculitis remains high despite normal brain blood vessel imaging by cerebral angiography, a brain biopsy should be strongly considered. [24] However, the sensitivity of biopsy is lower, and the specificity is higher. Biopsy specimens showing vasculitis can also reflect vasculitis from any cause and are not specific for PACNS.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Criteria
content: The diagnostic criteria for PACNS, formulated by Calabrese and Mallek, are used; a diagnosis is made if all 3 criteria are met. [27] These include the presence of an unexplained acquired neurologic deficit after extensive investigation for other causes, the presence of evidence of an inflammatory arteritic process within the CNS by either angiography or histopathological examination, or both; and no evidence of any other systemic vasculitis or any other disorders to which the angiographic or histopathologic features can be secondary. A diagnostic approach that combines the clinical, laboratory, and radiologic findings with angiography and, if required, biopsy is most prudent.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Criteria
content: Other essential evaluation tools include echocardiography, hypercoagulable evaluation with laboratory testing, eg, antiphospholipid antibodies, and blood cultures. An electrocardiogram or telemetry may be used to evaluate for arrhythmias. These studies are primarily aimed at ruling out other causes of PACNS mimics.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Treatment / Management
content: The treatment strategies for primary CNS vasculitis are primarily derived from case reports and cohort studies. In most patients, induction therapy is comprised of glucocorticoids alone or in combination with cyclophosphamide. The response rates for both monotherapy and combination therapy were similar, around 80%. The general recommendation is to start oral prednisone therapy promptly at the time of diagnosis at an initial dose of 1 mg/kg per day with a steroid-sparing medication. In most studies, cyclophosphamide is administered intravenously (IV) at a dose of 800 to 1000 mg/month for an average duration of 6 months. [7] In patients with more severe presentations, 1 g of methylprednisolone IV daily for 3 to 5 days, along with cyclophosphamide, can be used. However, the evidence of IV steroids being superior to an oral regimen has not been demonstrated. [28] [29] [30] [31] [32]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Treatment / Management
content: In cases of PACNS resistant to both glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, case reports describing rituximab, mycophenolic acid derivatives, azathioprine, methotrexate, and infliximab can be used as induction medications and/or maintenance medications while steroids are tapered. [7] Prophylactic therapy against Pneumocystis jirovecii and osteoporosis should be given to all patients, especially while patients remain on high doses of corticosteroids.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Treatment / Management
content: Maintenance therapy is typically with azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil. [18] The most common duration of maintenance therapy is 12 to 18 months. Monitoring is suggested at intervals of 1 to 2 months, with serial clinical exams and magnetic resonance imaging, performed at clinically appropriate intervals. [33] Reimaging of the CNS or other diagnostic testing, eg, a repeat lumbar puncture, should be strongly considered in the setting of clinical worsening or a change in status.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Differential Diagnosis
content: When evaluating a potential diagnosis of PACNS, clinicians must first exclude other disorders that can closely mimic its presentation. A comprehensive diagnostic evaluation to exclude these secondary causes must precede confirmation of PACNS, ensuring accurate diagnosis and appropriate management.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Differential Diagnosis -- Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome
content: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome frequently represents a major diagnostic challenge, often being mistaken for PACNS. Historically, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome has been described under various names, including Call-Fleming syndrome, migrainous vasospasm, postpartum angiopathy, benign angiopathy of the CNS, and CNS pseudovasculitis. The condition typically presents with a “thunderclap” headache triggered by factors, eg, high altitude, medications, medical procedures, or pregnancy.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Differential Diagnosis -- Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome
content: Differentiation from PACNS relies on its acute onset, normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and characteristic angiographic appearance of multifocal, segmental, centripetal narrowing and dilation of arteries that resolve within days to weeks. Imaging may reveal subarachnoid hemorrhage, watershed infarction, or cerebral edema. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome does not require immunosuppressive therapy. [34]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Differential Diagnosis -- Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy
content: CAA, a CNS disorder associated with amyloid deposition, can also mimic PACNS. [35] This age-related condition results from amyloid-β accumulation within the vessel walls of the leptomeninges and cortex and frequently occurs alongside Alzheimer’s disease. Amyloid-β weakens vessel walls, increasing the risk of rupture and bleeding. The inflammatory subtype of CAA manifests with subacute encephalopathy, headache, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits. CAA has 2 identified forms: cerebral amyloid angiopathy–related inflammation (CAAri), characterized by perivascular nondestructive inflammatory infiltrates, and amyloid-β–related angiitis, characterized by transmural, granulomatous vasculitic inflammation. The latter shares closer pathological features with PACNS. CAA-related disorders primarily affect older adults, in contrast to the typically younger PACNS population. [36]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Differential Diagnosis -- Other Differential Diagnoses
content: Secondary CNS vasculitis also encompasses a broad range of infectious, rheumatic, and autoinflammatory conditions capable of mimicking PACNS. The prototypical infectious cause, Varicella zoster virus, represents a classic imitator and should always be considered, especially in older or immunosuppressed patients. [37] Other infectious etiologies include bacterial pathogens, eg, Treponema pallidum (syphilis) and mycobacteria; viral infections, eg, Epstein-Barr virus and HIV; and fungal organisms, including Candida , Aspergillus , Histoplasma , Cryptococcus , and Nocardia . Rheumatic and autoinflammatory causes include granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), giant cell arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Behçet disease, and autoimmune encephalitis.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Differential Diagnosis -- Other Differential Diagnoses
content: Additional disorders capable of mimicking CNS vasculitis include Moyamoya disease, fibromuscular dysplasia, radiation vasculopathy, CNS lymphoma, intravascular lymphoma, and several genetic conditions. Drugs and toxins, eg, cocaine and amphetamines, as well as atherosclerosis, clotting disorders like antiphospholipid syndrome, and embolic events, may also produce similar clinical and radiologic findings.

Drugs and toxins, eg, cocaine and amphetamines, as well as atherosclerosis, clotting disorders like antiphospholipid syndrome, and embolic events, may also produce similar clinical and radiologic findings.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Prognosis
content: Approximately 26% to 27% of patients with PACNS may experience a relapse. [33] Prognostic factors portending a good outcome include an earlier time to diagnosis and better performance status at diagnosis, with fewer preexisting neurologic deficits. [38] [33] Factors associated with worse outcomes include poor medication tolerance, shorter intervals between recurrent symptoms, the presence of cognitive or behavioral abnormalities at diagnosis, and a wider range of lesions at diagnosis. [38] [14]

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Complications
content: Complications are due to neurologic deficits resulting from ischemic events distributed by the underlying vasculitis. The earlier the recognition and intervention, the better the outcomes tend to be. Other complications are secondary to medication adverse events. Infectious complications can result from both the use of steroids and steroid-sparing medications, some of which may be serious and life-threatening. Glucorticoid-induced osteoporosis, diabetes, weight gain, and hypertension are other potential adverse effects from longer-term use of steroids.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: PACNS is a rare condition, but it has a good prognosis when diagnosed early and treated promptly. Patients diagnosed with this condition need close monitoring while taking immunosuppressant medications. Patients should be advised of the importance of adhering to treatment, including medication, appointments, and laboratory monitoring, to improve outcomes. Reporting any adverse events to their clinicians, including symptoms of infection, worsening neurologic symptoms, or other potential adverse effects, should be done quickly. Participation in rehabilitation programs may be recommended to improve functional outcomes and should be encouraged. Management of comorbid conditions resulting from medication adverse effects is also essential and should be pursued in conjunction with the patient's primary care clinicians.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: PACNS is a rare, inflammatory disorder affecting the blood vessels of the brain and spinal cord, without systemic involvement. The disease presents with nonspecific and varied symptoms, including focal neurologic deficits, persistent headaches, cognitive decline, seizures, visual changes, and, occasionally, spinal cord involvement. Diagnosis requires careful evaluation, combining cerebrospinal fluid analysis, advanced neuroimaging, and, when indicated, brain biopsy, while ruling out secondary causes of CNS vasculitis. Prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, typically with glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, followed by maintenance therapy, is essential to improve patient outcomes. Ongoing monitoring through clinical assessment and imaging helps guide therapy adjustments and detect relapses.

title: Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of PACNS relies on an interprofessional approach. Physicians and advanced practitioners lead diagnostic evaluation and treatment planning, while nurses support symptom monitoring, patient education, and therapy administration. Radiology, interventional radiology, neurosurgery, and pathology play a critical role in obtaining and interpreting key diagnostic data in those evaluations. Patients are typically affected by lasting neurologic deficits requiring rehabilitation, physical, occupational, and speech therapy, and physical medicine and rehabilitation are also very important members of the care team, leading to improved long-term outcomes. Pharmacists ensure safe and effective use of immunosuppressive medications and prophylactic therapies. Interprofessional communication and care coordination allow timely recognition of complications, adjustment of therapy, and comprehensive support for patients and families, ultimately enhancing patient-centered care, safety, and team performance in managing this complex neurologic disorder.
